ask: Black played ...e5 without ...a6 first. How does White make that hurt?
text: The ...a6 move takes b5 away from White's pieces, prepares ...b5 and keeps the setup flexible, which is why an immediate ...e5 is premature (Bb5+ is unpleasant). In the English attack structure the kings usually castle on opposite wings, so Black's main plan is a queenside pawn advance with ...b5, ...b4, ...a5 and ...a4 to strip away the pieces covering White's king. The knight normally belongs on d7, and Black must be careful not to allow a4 before pushing ...b5.

text: In the Tartakower line (after Nd2, ...dxe4, Nxe4, ...Nf6, Nxf6+) recapture with ...exf6, not ...gxf6. Black accepts a damaged structure in return for easy development: the bishop goes to d6, then ...Bg4 ties down a white knight on f3, and White must either weaken with h3 and g4 or retreat the bishop to e2 passively. Do not pick a line only because it leads to one appealing position, since you also need a plan against White's other options, above all the Advance.

text: Black's ...c5 with ...Qb6 is the standard way to unsettle the London, because the early bishop leaves b2 loose.
